posts.quote: A COLD MEANT A DAB OF VAPOR RUB, A WARM FLANNEL, AND MOM'S HAND ON YOUR FOREHEAD ALL NIGHT.
posts.caption: When you caught a cold, the whole house rearranged itself around you. Mom warmed a flannel cloth on the radiator and laid it across your chest over a thick smear of that menthol rub, and the smell filled the room before the heat ever reached you. The bedroom door stayed open a hand's width so she could hear you breathe. A glass of water and a box of tissues sat on the chair, and the little lamp stayed on low. Sometime past midnight you felt a cool hand on your forehead, and you pretended to be asleep so she wouldn't stop.
posts.first: Mine always checked my forehead with the back of her hand, never the front. She said the back of the hand knew more. I still do it the same way, and nobody in my house has ever argued with the result.

posts.quote: THE KITCHEN TIMER TICKED LOUD ENOUGH TO HEAR FROM THE YARD, AND WHEN IT RANG EVERY KID WAS SUDDENLY HUNGRY.
posts.caption: The timer sat on the counter next to the stove, a round white dial with a little bell inside, and Mom wound it with one twist of her wrist. It ticked steadily through every pie, roast, and pan of rolls, loud enough to hear from the back steps. Nobody said what was cooking, but kids drifted into the kitchen anyway and stood around pretending to look for something. When the bell finally rang, it was a small flat clatter, and Mom had the oven door open before it finished. That was the whole signal, and the house understood it.
posts.first: Ours had a chip in the white paint where somebody dropped it on the linoleum. It kept perfect time anyway, or close enough that nobody ever checked. I still have it in a drawer, and it still rings.

posts.quote: THE AUCTIONEER / A SINGSONG PATTER, A BOX LOT, AND A SCRATCH OF THE NOSE THAT COST YOU TEN DOLLARS
posts.caption: The farm auction started at ten sharp, and the auctioneer was already talking before he climbed onto the hay wagon. His patter ran together into a song nobody could follow, but the old farmers in the front row never missed a number. Folding chairs lined the lawn, and the church ladies sold pie and coffee from the back of a station wagon. Somebody always paid a dollar for a box of mystery and went home with a hammer, a doorknob, and half a set of dishes. The kids were warned not to scratch their nose, wave at a friend, or sneeze, because the man on the wagon saw everything.
posts.first: My uncle once bought a pump organ because he swatted a fly at the wrong second. It sat in his barn for thirty years. He swore he never played a note, but I caught him at the keys more than once.
